extracted.intended_audience: writers, students, and general readers interested in narrative theory and story-craft
extracted.subtask_description: A broad encyclopedic overview of narrative/story structure types, components, and historical theories that writers and students can use to understand or plan the ordering and functions of events in a story. Covers models (three‑act, kishōtenketsu, Freytag), narration types (linear, nonlinear, interactive), and genre-specific forms (graphic narrative).

rubrics_metrics.name: Story structure (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Story structure or narrative structure is the recognizable or comprehensible way in which a narrative's different elements are unified, including in a particularly chosen order and sometimes specifically referring to the ordering of the plot: the narrative series of events. Story is a sequence of events, which can be true or fictitious, that appear in prose, verse or script, designed to amuse and/or inform an audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Story structure organizes a story's elements into a recognizable sequence and has been shown to influence how the brain organizes information. Structures can vary by culture and historical period; the same named structure may change over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-act structure (overall)
rubrics_metrics.description: A common structure in classical film and other Western-associated narrative forms that divides a story into three parts: beginning (first act), middle (second act), and end (third act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Popularized by Syd Field and historically connected to earlier commentators. The three acts map to setup/exposition, confrontation, and resolution; the model emphasizes progression through two major plot points and a central dramatic question.

rubrics_metrics.name: First act — setup / exposition and inciting incident
rubrics_metrics.description: The first act begins with setup, where all the main characters and their basic situations are introduced as well as the setting; this setup is often called the exposition. Later in the first act the protagonist experiences a dynamic event known as the inciting incident (or catalyst).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First-act purpose: introduce characters, relationships, world dynamics and provide primary characterization. The inciting incident provokes initial actions to deal with change and attempts to reestablish order, leading to the first plot point that raises the dramatic question (example: 'Will X disable the bomb?').

rubrics_metrics.name: Second act — confrontation and character development (character arc)
rubrics_metrics.description: The second act, or confrontation, is considered the bulk of the story where the characters' conflict is most developed (particularly between protagonist and antagonist) and where changes in values and personality (character development or character arc) occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This act deepens conflict and tests characters, driving toward the second plot point that transitions into the resolution and the protagonist's return (or movement) toward an ending.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third act — resolution and climax
rubrics_metrics.description: The third act, or resolution, is when the problem in the story escalates, forcing characters to confront it and allowing elements to come together, leading to the climax, which answers the dramatic question and concludes the conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Third-act purpose: bring stakes to a head, resolve the dramatic question, and show consequences; it completes the arc set up earlier in the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot point / dramatic question (inciting incident → plot point → climax linkage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Key structural moments: an inciting incident/catalyst initiates change, a plot point (first plot point) ends the first act and raises a dramatic question, and the climax (typically in the third act) answers that dramatic question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dramatic question is an organizing device that propels the reader/viewer (example phrasing offered: 'Will X disable the bomb?' or 'Will Y end up with their love interest?'). Plot points mark act boundaries and shift the story's direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kishōtenketsu (four-part Eastern structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: A four-part structure derived from classic Chinese, Korean, and Japanese narratives: typically divided into introduction, development (or beginning of self-realization/action), a turning point/reversal/twist, and a result or conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each culture uses the form differently, but the common roles are: (1) introduction, (2) development/beginning of action or self-realization, (3) turning point/change/reversal, (4) consequence/coming to fruition. It emphasizes development and twist rather than conflict-driven escalation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freytag's Pyramid / five-part dramatic structure
rubrics_metrics.description: A historical five-part plot diagram outlining: Introduction, Rise, Climax, Return or Fall, and Catastrophe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freytag's scheme influenced later models (including three- and five-act structures). It is useful for mapping rising action, peak, and aftermath, particularly in analyses of classical and 19th‑century drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linear narrative (chronological)
rubrics_metrics.description: Linear narrative presents events largely in chronological order, telling events in the order in which they occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Linear format is most common. Techniques like flashbacks may be used, but they usually exist within an overall linear framework (flashbacks still rely on a fundamentally linear understanding).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonlinear narrative (broken chronology)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonlinear, disjointed, or disrupted narratives portray events out of chronological order or employ structures that do not follow direct causality patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include films like Pulp Fiction, which break chronology to reorder sections of a single story; novels may also arrange chapters non-chronologically to achieve literary effects (spirals, waves, meanders).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interactive narration (delivery-driven interaction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Narration in which the linear narrative is driven by the user's interaction: the delivery method requires the user to actively work to gain the next piece of the narrative (e.g., by reaching objectives, solving puzzles, or completing levels).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common in some modern video games; the narrative advances only as the user accomplishes tasks, creating a sense of progression tied to gameplay rather than branching choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interactive narrative (branching/choice-driven)
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrative composed with a branching structure where a single starting point may lead to multiple developments and outcomes; at each step the user makes choices that advance the story toward different series of choices and endings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authoring interactive narratives implies imagining many parallel stories. Typical forms include gamebooks (readers turn to pages based on choices) and branching video games; choices are typically action-based rather than conversational, and improvisational theatre is open-ended though not strictly authored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graphic narrative — four stages (suitable for comics and simple sequential art)
rubrics_metrics.description: A simple graphic narrative has four stages: (1) introduction of characters and situation; (2) introduction of a problem, unexpected opportunity, or complication; (3) a resolution as a response by characters; (4) denouement showing aftermath and how the original situation has changed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In simple narratives the four stages appear in order; in complex stories the order of telling may vary (e.g., beginning with denouement and using flashback). The fourth stage clarifies success/partial success/failure or uncertainty of the response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character development / character arc as structural criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Character development (character arc) refers to changes in values and personality one or more characters undergo during the story; this is a central structural purpose of the confrontation/bulk of the narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Second-act emphasis: conflict should produce believable changes in the protagonist (and other characters) that justify the climax and resolution; building character through psychology, sociology, and physiology is a noted method.
